Everyone says Africa needs more capital. That framing is wrong — and it is costing founders their best years.

The real problem, as Modern Diplomacy's analysis of Africa's capital continuum makes clear, is not the total volume of money. It is the missing middle.

Seed rounds exist. Large infrastructure and DFI capital exists. What is structurally absent is the growth-stage layer — the Series A and B capital that converts a validated startup into a scalable, bankable business.

Without that bridge:
→ Early investors cannot recycle returns into the next cohort
→ Founders plateau at proof-of-concept for years
→ DFI infrastructure investments land in ecosystems too thin to absorb them

The World Bank's recent work on African integration adds a second dimension: even where growth capital does exist, regulatory fragmentation means it rarely crosses borders efficiently. A fund domiciled in Nairobi faces genuine structural friction deploying into Lagos or Accra.

So the capital is not just missing — it is also trapped.

The fix is not another fund announcement. It is the connective tissue: blended finance facilities that de-risk mid-stage deals for global allocators, regional guarantee schemes, and cross-border regulatory harmonisation that makes African growth equity legible on a global term sheet.

Volume without sequencing is noise.

sources_used.title: How the AI Investment Craze Is Keeping the Global Economy Afloat - WSJ
Integrating Africa: From Threads to Hubs - World Bank Group

pages.markdown:
Twelve months ago, the global economy looked fragile. Today, one sector is quietly keeping it together — and almost nobody is talking about the geographic fault line it is creating.

The WSJ's analysis makes the case clearly: AI investment — data centres, semiconductor supply chains, model infrastructure — has become a macroeconomic stabiliser. It is absorbing capital, sustaining employment, and propping up growth readings in economies that would otherwise be contracting.

Before this AI capex cycle: the global economy was navigating post-rate-hike slowdown with few obvious growth engines.

After: a concentrated wave of private and corporate investment in AI infrastructure is doing the work that fiscal stimulus used to do.

That is a remarkable shift. But here is what the macro framing misses.

The World Bank's recent work on African integration highlights that the infrastructure Africa needs to participate in the AI economy — reliable power, fibre connectivity, technical education — is not being funded at anything close to the same velocity as GPU clusters in Virginia or data centres in Singapore.

The result: AI investment is keeping the global economy afloat, but it is simultaneously redrawing the map of which economies will benefit from the next productivity cycle.

For investors and operators thinking about long-term positioning:
→ AI capex is a macro tailwind — but it is geographically concentrated
→ The foundational infrastructure gap in emerging markets is widening, not closing
→ The window to shape AI's geographic distribution is now, not after the infrastructure is built

If AI investment is the new infrastructure spend keeping the global economy afloat, who is responsible for ensuring the next wave reaches economies that need it most — governments, DFIs, or the private sector?
